Regarding the definition of "zero-shot generalization" in the context of text-to-image AIs, it's a sensible concept. Zero-shot generalization refers to the ability of a model to apply its learned knowledge to new, unseen concepts without requiring any additional training data. In other words, the model can generalize to novel classes or concepts without having seen any examples of those classes before.

This definition is relevant to text-to-image AIs because these models are trained on large datasets of text-image pairs, where the text describes an image. The model learns to associate certain words or phrases with specific visual features or objects. When presented with a new, unseen text, the model should be able to apply its learned knowledge to generate an image that matches the description, even if it's never seen that specific text before.

The 2013 paper that defines zero-shot generalization likely discussed the challenges and limitations of achieving this goal in text-to-image AIs. The concept is closely related to the idea of "few-shot learning," where a model is trained on a small number of examples and can generalize to new, unseen data.

Some researchers have explored the concept of zero-shot generalization in text-to-image AIs, and there are ongoing efforts to develop models that can achieve this goal. However, it remains an open research question, and significant challenges need to be addressed before text-to-image AIs can truly demonstrate zero-shot generalization.
